first-90-days-in-austin-as-an-internatio.title: First 90 days in Austin as an international founder
first-90-days-in-austin-as-an-internatio.description: Housing, neighborhoods, documents, and local ops peers at IFN Austin talk through so the company survives landing.
first-90-days-in-austin-as-an-internatio.html:
Austin's in-person meetups often have one founder holding a phone with a map open, asking the room which part of town they should actually live in. They landed two weeks ago. The company is formed, the bank account is half open, and they have spent their first ten days in a short-term rental. They are trying to work out whether to sign a twelve-month lease before they know where they will spend most of their time. Someone across the table laughs, because they asked the same question a year earlier.

This is peer orientation from that room: where people live, which documents everyone ends up scrambling for, and how to keep the company running while your personal life is still in boxes. Not a relocation checklist. Not a substitute for counsel.

Disclaimer

This is not legal, tax, immigration, housing, or banking advice. IFN shares what founders in the room tend to talk through. Lease rules, fair housing questions, tax residency, and status limits change with your facts. Verify with licensed professionals and official sources before you act.

First weeks versus first 90 days

Founders who have been through it describe two different jobs.

The first few weeks are about landing. You need a place to sleep, a working phone number, a way to get around, and a mailing address that will still be valid next month. Most people underestimate how much of this depends on documents they left in a drawer back home.

The first 90 days are about making sure the company survives the move. Payroll, invoices, bank logins, registered agent mail, and investor updates all keep going whether or not you have furniture. Peers who struggled usually let the company side drift while they sorted out housing, then spent a month catching up.

A pattern the room keeps returning to is to treat these as three separate tracks:

  1. Personal landing (housing, phone, transport, your own ID and paperwork)
  2. Company paper (entity, registered agent, state filings, contracts)
  3. Money rails (business banking, payment processors, how money moves between your home country and the US entity)

They overlap, but they break in different ways. A lease delay should not hold up a payroll run, and a bank asking for proof of address should not stop you signing a customer. Keeping the tracks apart in your notes makes it easier to see which one is actually stuck.

Housing patterns peers talk about

Nobody in the room will hand you a ranking of neighborhoods, and you should be wary of anyone who does. What you will hear instead are patterns.

Short-term first, lease second. Many founders start with a furnished short-term place for a month or two, then sign a longer lease once they know where they will spend their days. The trade-off is cost and some instability against making a twelve-month commitment before you know the city.

Roommate or solo. Some newcomers share a place with another founder or a professional they meet through the community, which can make lease approval easier when you do not have US credit history. Others need a quiet solo setup for late calls across time zones. Both are common. The right choice depends on your work hours more than anything else.

Neighborhoods people mention. A few areas come up again and again in conversation, each for its own reasons:

  • Downtown, near Station Austin at 701 Brazos St. Walkable to coworking, meetups, and a lot of daytime meetings. People mention it when they want to live close to where the founder community gathers.
  • East Austin. Founders bring it up for residential streets, cafes, and proximity to downtown.
  • North Austin and the Domain side. It comes up among people who work with larger tech employers up north or want more space.
  • The South Congress corridor. People mention it for its own neighborhood feel and easy access back into downtown.

Prices, availability, and how people feel about each area change. Talk to people who live there now before you decide. Bring your actual constraints to the meetup (car or no car, how often you need to be downtown, budget range) and you will get far more useful answers than "where should I live?"

Documents people scramble for

Almost everyone in the room has a story about a document they did not think they would need.

Passport and status paperwork. Keep copies in more than one place. You will be asked for ID constantly in the first month: for leases, phone plans, banks, and sometimes building access.

Lease or proof of address. Banks, utilities, and some government processes ask for proof that you live where you say you live. Founders in short-term rentals sometimes find this harder than expected. Ask early what your landlord or host can provide in writing.

SSN or ITIN. This comes up as a peer operations note, not advice. Some people are eligible for a Social Security number based on their status. Others who are not may need an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number for certain tax purposes. Which one applies to you, and when, depends on your facts. Start at the IRS ITIN page and the Social Security Administration number and card page. If you are unsure which applies, that is a question for a professional.

Company documents, separate from personal ones. Formation papers, EIN confirmation, and operating or governance documents belong to the company track. Peers suggest keeping them in their own folder so you are not digging through lease PDFs during a bank call.

Local operations

Getting around. Austin is spread out. Some founders downtown get by on walking, rideshare, and public transit for a while. Others decide quickly that they need a car, which brings its own questions about licenses and insurance. Check official Texas sources for licensing rules that apply to your situation rather than relying on what worked for a friend.

Phone and utilities. A US phone number early on helps with almost everything, from two-factor codes to landlord calls. Utility setup depends on your building and address, so ask your landlord what is already included.

A place to work. Many international founders use Station Austin at 701 Brazos St for coworking, especially in the first months when home is not set up yet. You also end up around other founders, which matters when you do not know anyone yet.

Getting to the IFN meetup. The IFN monthly in-person meetup for international and immigrant founders happens at Station Austin. Newcomers who come in their first month or two tend to find the landing goes faster, because they can ask about a landlord, a bank, or a document problem and usually find someone who has dealt with it.

When we stop talking

Call licensed professionals when any of these show up:

  • Immigration status questions, including what your visa allows you to do with your company, travel plans, and timing
  • Housing discrimination or lease disputes that escalate beyond peer tips
  • Tax residency questions: when you become a US tax resident, how that interacts with your home country, and how it affects your company

Immigration counsel, a housing or civil attorney when needed, and a CPA with cross-border experience are different seats.

Soft next steps

Come to the next IFN meetup with one concrete landing question: a neighborhood you are weighing, a document a bank asked for, or a lease decision you are stuck on. Guests are welcome; register on Luma or check dates on ifn.community. If you want the private member channel and members-only call, Become a member. Fuller relocation checklists and city notes live with membership and the Resources hub as that catalog fills in.

Sources

  • IRS, Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN)
  • Social Security Administration, Social Security number and card
  • Station Austin, stationaustin.org

forming-a-us-company-from-abroad.title: Forming a US company from abroad: what peers actually sequence
forming-a-us-company-from-abroad.description: What international founders at IFN Austin tend to sequence when forming a US company from abroad, and when they stop and call counsel.
forming-a-us-company-from-abroad.html:
At almost every IFN Austin meetup, someone still abroad asks the same cluster: Can I form a United States company before I have work authorization? LLC or C-corp? Which state? When does the EIN happen? How do people avoid confusing formation with permission to work?

This is peer sequencing from that room. Not a filing checklist. Not a substitute for counsel.

Disclaimer

This is not legal, tax, immigration, or banking advice. IFN shares what founders in the room tend to talk through. Entity choice, tax elections, beneficial ownership reporting, and immigration consequences change with your facts. Verify with licensed professionals and official sources (IRS, your state filing office, FinCEN) before you act.

Three tracks peers try to keep separate

Forming a US company is not the same as being authorized to work in the United States.

Founders who have been through it often separate three tracks early:

  1. Company paper (entity, registered agent, EIN, ownership docs)
  2. Personal status (visa, work authorization, travel)
  3. Money rails (banking, payments, how customers pay)

Mixing those tracks is where people get surprised. Formation can happen while you are still abroad. Work authorization is a different conversation. Banking prep is another. Meetup peers talk about all three; counsel owns the hard calls on each.

What people tend to sequence (high level)

No two founders run the same order. A pattern still shows up often enough that newcomers ask for it:

  1. Decide what job the entity has to do in the next 12 to 24 months (raise, serve US customers from abroad, support a later visa conversation without inventing eligibility, or keep a simple operating company). Peer pattern talk, not a recommendation. Cooley's June 2025 note on US visas and corporate structure is useful orientation; your advisors still own the call.

  2. Pick a formation state as an ops decision, not a brand decision. Delaware shows up because investors and counsel know it. Other states show up for cost or stack. Texas shows up when people already live or plan to live in Austin. Consistency with what you later show banks matters more than the logo on the filing. Delaware's Division of Corporations publishes how to form a new business entity; your own state's filing office is the source for non-Delaware filings.

  3. File, freeze the legal name, then get an EIN. Banks and the IRS notice character-level name mismatches. Founders abroad often learn online EIN eligibility depends on US presence and a suitable taxpayer ID for the responsible party. Start at the IRS EIN overview and Form SS-4 instructions.

  4. Keep ownership clear, and check current FinCEN BOI rules for your facts. Rules have changed. Start at FinCEN BOI reporting and FAQs, then ask counsel whether your facts still create a filing duty.

  5. Only then move toward banking. Incomplete company paper is an expensive way to learn. Peers gather formation evidence, EIN confirmation, ownership clarity, and a real operating address before they apply. The item-by-item pack language lives deeper with membership and Resources, not in this orientation post.

LLC vs C-corp as founders discuss it

In meetup language, LLCs get described as lighter early governance. Delaware C-corps get described as the default language for US venture conversations. Tax elections are not peer DIY. Structure and equity can interact with visa strategy, so corporate and immigration counsel often need to coordinate.

When we stop talking

Call licensed professionals when any of these show up:

  • You need a recommendation on LLC versus C-corp for your personal tax residency
  • Equity, vesting, or board control might interact with a visa strategy
  • You are unsure whether FinCEN BOI still applies to your entity
  • A formation service's marketing copy conflicts with IRS or state instructions
  • You are treating company formation as proof you can work in the US

Corporate counsel, immigration counsel, and a CPA who has worked with non-resident founders are different seats.

Soft next steps

Come to the next IFN meetup with one concrete formation question. Guests are welcome; register on Luma or check dates on ifn.community. If you want the private member channel and members-only call, Become a member. Fuller formation checklists and teaser PDFs live with membership and the Resources hub as that catalog fills in.

Sources

  • IRS, Employer identification number
  • IRS, Instructions for Form SS-4
  • Delaware Division of Corporations, How to form a new business entity
  • FinCEN, Beneficial Ownership Information Reporting
  • FinCEN, BOI FAQs
  • Cooley, What Foreign Founders Need to Know About US Visas and Corporate Structure (orientation; not IFN advice)

us-business-banking-document-pack.title: US business banking for international founders: what peers gather first
us-business-banking-document-pack.description: What international founders at IFN tend to gather before they walk into a US business banking conversation, at overview level.
us-business-banking-document-pack.html:
After formation and EIN talk, banking is the next wall at IFN Austin meetups. Founders often say they assumed the hard part was "being foreign." What they describe afterward sounds more like incomplete company paper: mismatched names, a registered-agent address used as the operating address, missing EIN confirmation, or ownership docs that do not match passport spellings.

This is peer orientation on what people tend to gather before they walk into a bank or remote onboarding flow. It is not a downloadable checklist, not a promise any bank will approve you, and not product endorsement. The fuller pack language belongs with membership and Resources.

Disclaimer

This is not banking, legal, tax, or immigration advice. Bank and fintech policies change. Underwriting is individual. Verify requirements with the institution you apply to. IFN shares patterns from founder conversations, not guarantees.

The wrong wall, in meetup language

A common story in the room: form a US LLC or C-corp from abroad, upload a passport and Articles PDF to a remote business account, get stalled or declined, then conclude "US banks do not want internationals."

Peers who cleared remote onboarding usually rewrite that story: the underwriter could not reconcile an incomplete company file. Nationality still matters for some products. Incomplete paper fails more often than founders expect.

Industry examples (not IFN endorsements): Mercury's How to open a U.S. bank account remotely and OtoCo's 2026 foreign-owned LLC banking guide. Your bank's checklist still wins.

What peers tend to gather (overview, not a pack)

Every institution differs. At a high level, founders who later cleared onboarding usually had these categories ready before they applied:

  • Formation evidence with the exact legal name, state, and filing date. Entity choice and sequencing are a separate peer conversation; keep company paper frozen before you apply.
  • EIN confirmation that matches that legal name. IRS EIN overview and Form SS-4 instructions.
  • Ownership and signing authority clear enough that beneficial owners and control persons are not a mid-review surprise.
  • Government IDs for owners and control persons, with names that match formation docs.
  • A real business mailing or principal place of business address, separate from the registered agent used only for service of process. Many remote underwriters reject registered-agent-only or PO box-only addresses. Check yours.
  • A boring, true business description. Vague activity language creates manual review. Inventing a safer-sounding industry creates a worse problem later.

That is orientation, not a fillable inventory. The item-by-item pack and member-channel walkthroughs live deeper in Resources and with membership.

Remote path vs traditional path

Remote path: browser upload plus review. Peers report stalls when the address is the registered agent, the EIN name mismatches, beneficial ownership is incomplete, or the activity is unsupported.

Traditional path: denser KYC, longer timelines, sometimes an in-person step. Branch visits with Articles alone often burn the trip.

Product names come and go. Re-read current eligibility pages, including any prohibited-residence list, before you build plans on a forum thread.

SSN, ITIN, and a separate visa track

In many remote stories, the company is the customer and controlling persons provide passport KYC. An SSN is not always required for the company account. An ITIN is personal; it is not a substitute for the company's EIN. Some banks still want a US person with signing authority.

Visa status is a separate track. Owning a US company is not permission to work in the United States. Keep personal status questions for immigration counsel, not for the banking underwriter.

When we stop talking

Call a professional or the bank's support channel when:

  • You need a product recommendation for your facts
  • Your industry or residence may be unsupported
  • Names or addresses already conflict across docs
  • Someone suggests misstating activity to pass review
  • Tax residency or payroll setup enters the chat
  • A decline letter needs interpretation against your KYC file

Meetup peers can share what they assembled. They cannot underwrite you.

Soft next steps

Bring your banking-prep questions (not your passport data) to the next IFN meetup. Guests are welcome; register on Luma or check ifn.community. For the private member channel, members-only call, and the fuller banking pack / teaser PDF language as it ships, Become a member or browse Resources.

Sources

  • Mercury, How to open a U.S. bank account remotely
  • OtoCo, How to Open a US Bank Account for a Foreign-Owned LLC (2026 Guide)
  • IRS, Employer identification number
  • IRS, Instructions for Form SS-4

visa-paths-founders-talk-about-at-ifn.title: Visa paths founders talk about at IFN (and when we stop talking)
visa-paths-founders-talk-about-at-ifn.description: A peer map of visa paths founders discuss at IFN meetups, and the moments the room hands the conversation to immigration counsel.
visa-paths-founders-talk-about-at-ifn.html:
Visa questions arrive early at IFN Austin meetups. Someone is still on a student timeline. Someone else is abroad and wondering whether to form a company first. Someone on an employer-sponsored status asks what they can do for a side project without putting their status at risk.

This is a peer orientation map of the paths that come up in the room. IFN does not file petitions. IFN does not tell you which visa you qualify for.

Disclaimer

This is not immigration, legal, tax, or banking advice. USCIS, the Department of State, and licensed immigration counsel are the authorities for eligibility, petitions, and status decisions. Rules change. Your facts matter. Use this only as meetup-shaped orientation, then verify with professionals and official pages before you act.

How the room talks about visas

Founders at IFN tend to talk in paths and constraints:

  • What status am I on now?
  • What am I allowed to do for a company I own?
  • What would a change of status or a consular application require?
  • Who petitions: me, my company, an employer, or a family member?
  • When do I stop brainstorming and hire counsel?

Peer stories help you ask better questions. They do not replace a case assessment. A careful public overview is Cooley's June 2025 note on foreign founders, visas, and corporate structure. Read it as orientation. Your attorney still owns your case.

The room also compares notes on timing: when to talk to counsel relative to incorporation, fundraising, or a planned trip. That timing talk stays peer pattern. It is never a filing calendar.

Paths that come up often (names + official links only)

The names below are classifications founders discuss at meetups. Official pages are linked so you can read primary language yourself. IFN does not score eligibility or assemble evidence packages.

  • O-1. Comes up when founders have a dense record of recognition in a defined field. The moment anyone asks "do I have enough evidence?" the room stops. USCIS O-1.
  • E-2. Comes up for nationals of qualifying treaty countries, usually alongside investment and ownership questions that are fact-specific. Check the treaty list first. USCIS E-2, Treaty Countries.
  • H-1B. Comes up around lottery calendars, employer-specific limits, and founder-owned company questions. IFN does not draw that line. USCIS H-1B.
  • L-1. Comes up when there is already a real foreign operating company, not only an idea. USCIS L-1A, L-1B.
  • Student and visitor timelines (F-1, OPT, B-1/B-2). Ownership and active work are different questions. As soon as the question becomes "am I allowed to do X on my current status?" the meetup conversation ends.
  • Green card / EB conversations. Peer orientation only. Counsel early. No eligibility theater.

Formation and visas are linked, but not the same project

A recurring IFN lesson: people form a US company and then assume the visa problem is solved. It is not.

Company paper and personal status move on different clocks. Peers who stay calm tend to keep a written list of what their current status allows, form the entity only when it serves a clear ops or fundraising job, gather banking materials after the entity exists, and book immigration counsel before they restructure equity "for a visa story."

When we stop talking

Call immigration counsel when:

  • You want a recommendation among O-1, E-2, H-1B, L-1, or any other path
  • You need evidence strategy, petition drafting, or consular prep
  • Your nationality, dual citizenship, or prior refusals change the map
  • You are on student or visitor status and want a green light for active work
  • Equity, board control, or vesting might be rearranged for status reasons
  • Someone offers you a "guaranteed" petition path in a group chat

IFN is a peer room. Counsel is a licensed professional with your facts and your file.

Soft next steps

Bring one status question to the next IFN meetup. Guests stay free via the meetup; register on Luma or see dates on ifn.community. If you want the private member channel and members-only call, Become a member. Deeper visa pathway maps and teaser PDFs live with membership and Resources as that hub fills in.

Sources

  • USCIS, O-1
  • USCIS, E-2
  • USCIS, H-1B
  • USCIS, L-1A
  • USCIS, L-1B
  • US Department of State, Treaty Countries
  • Cooley, US visas and corporate structure (orientation; not IFN advice)

welcome-to-the-ifn-blog.title: Welcome to the IFN blog
welcome-to-the-ifn-blog.description: Peer notes from IFN meetups in Austin for international founders. Field notes you can read before you walk into the room.
welcome-to-the-ifn-blog.html:
IFN runs a free monthly meetup in Austin for international and immigrant founders. The same questions show up every month: how people register a company in the United States, how they stay inside visa limits while they build, how they open a bank account, and how local funding conversations differ from the ones they had at home.

This blog is where we write those conversations down. Not legal advice. Not a course. Peer experience from founders who are doing the work in Austin, so you can arrive at the next meetup with sharper questions.

What you will find here

  • Field notes from the room: what surprised people who just landed, and what they wish they had asked earlier.
  • Orientation on visas, entity setup, banking, housing, hiring, and fundraising as an international founder, always as peer framing. When a topic needs counsel, we say so.
  • Soft pointers to the next meetup, the optional membership (private member channel and members-only call), and the Resources hub when a catalog title is useful.

What this is not

This is not the paid Resources library. Guides that belong behind membership stay there. The blog stays free to read.

It is also not a newsletter signup page. When we publish, the post lives at /blog. Come to a meetup if you want the live version of the same conversation.

Start here

If you are new to Austin as an international founder, come to the next meetup first. Register on Luma. Bring one concrete question. The blog will keep adding the written version of what the room keeps teaching.
